The World Is Your Driveway

The brilliant rise of campervan swapping, $1 road trips, and the art of seeing the world without buying another RV.

By Priya Raghavan · 20 minute read

Imagine owning a campervan in California. Nothing extravagant. Maybe a converted Mercedes Sprinter, a Volkswagen Eurovan, or an aging Ford Econoline that has crossed more state lines than most people cross streets. It is your little piece of freedom. It has a bed, a refrigerator, some questionable cabinet hinges, and enough memories to make selling it almost impossible.

Now imagine waking up one morning and deciding you want to spend 6 weeks driving through New Zealand. There is just 1 problem. Your campervan is in California, New Zealand is roughly 6,500 miles away, and the Pacific Ocean has a rather inconvenient policy regarding road travel.

Traditionally, you had 3 options: rent another campervan, ship yours overseas, or abandon the idea and book hotels. But there is a 4th option, and it might be one of the most brilliant ideas in recreational motoring. Swap your campervan with somebody who already owns one where you want to go.

You drive theirs. They drive yours. Both parties get a vehicle and a place to sleep, potentially saving thousands of dollars. No buying, no selling, no ocean crossing for either vehicle.

And the best part? This is not merely a clever idea waiting for somebody to invent it. Several companies have already built platforms around it: RV Worldwide, Swap My Van, and SwapTheRoad. Then there are alternatives such as Imoova, which effectively covers part of your travel costs by offering remarkably cheap one-way vehicle relocations. And for the dedicated traveler who refuses to drive anything other than their own beloved motorhome, companies like American Lamprecht and SeaBridge will put the whole thing on a ship. 3 fundamentally different approaches, 1 wonderfully simple objective: make the world accessible through the windshield of a vehicle.

Part One: The Great Campervan Exchange

Think about the basic economics. You already own a campervan. Somebody in Australia also owns a campervan. Both vehicles spend a substantial amount of time parked, doing absolutely nothing except depreciating and occasionally attracting bird droppings.

You want to visit Australia. The Australian owner wants to visit the United States. Why should both of you spend thousands renting vehicles while 2 perfectly usable campers remain parked at home?

It is the same principle behind home exchanges, except the house can move. There is something especially appealing about that distinction. You're not simply borrowing accommodation; you're inheriting somebody else's passport to adventure.

A motorhome in Scotland could introduce you to Highland roads and isolated lochs. A compact camper in France could take you through Alpine villages and onto the Mediterranean coast. A rugged 4x4 camper in Australia could open up the Outback. And your own campervan, meanwhile, is showing another traveler the Pacific Coast Highway, Yosemite, or the American Southwest.

Neither vehicle crosses an ocean. The people do.

The concept also creates an interesting kind of trust. Most enthusiasts would be reluctant to hand their keys to a complete stranger, especially when the keys belong to something they have spent years maintaining and modifying. But recreational-vehicle owners have something in common: they understand the machine is more than transportation.

That mutual understanding is the foundation upon which these platforms operate. It does not eliminate risk, but it makes the idea far more plausible than it might initially sound.

Part Two: 3 Companies, 3 Ways to See the World

1. RV Worldwide — The Established Veteran

RV Worldwide

Best for planned international exchanges

Established 2008 · US$79.90 annual membership · 830 members

A community-oriented platform for owners who want to arrange substantial trips and build relationships with other travelers.

rvworldwide.com

RV Worldwide is the veteran of the group. Founded in 2008, it has spent nearly 2 decades connecting owners around the world, and the site reports 830 members as of November 2026. This isn't a service where you click a button and somebody hands you the keys to a Winnebago in Italy tomorrow morning. It is closer to joining an international travel club.

For $79.90 a year, members list their vehicles, communicate with other owners, and arrange exchanges directly. The fee covers as many exchanges as you can arrange during the membership year, and the company says it will extend your membership free of charge until you secure a first exchange if none materializes in the first 12 months.

Perhaps most importantly, exchanges don't have to happen at the same time. A European owner could use your camper during the American summer, and you could use theirs months later; RV Worldwide says exchanges between hemispheres often end up about 6 months apart. The company even recommends joining and listing your vehicle 12 months before an intended international trip. That is particularly appealing for retired couples, families planning extended vacations, and anyone who believes 3 weeks in another country is barely enough time to figure out where the good bakeries are.

A real exchange story

Barbara and Mike, an English couple, first wrote up their swaps for RV Worldwide in 2018 and updated the story in June 2026. By then they had completed 6 exchanges of 2 to 3 months each with couples in New Zealand and Australia. The first was 8 weeks in a Sunshine Coast couple's motorhome, working up the Queensland coast from Brisbane to the Daintree. The Australians didn't collect their half of the deal for 5 years, thanks to Covid and work, and when they finally did, they took the English couple's motorhome across to Ireland for 2 months with a small Fiat on tow.

The swaps that followed, with couples from Tauranga, Napier and Whakatane, turned into friendships. When a planned exchange with a Wellington owner fell apart, the Tauranga couple handed over their own van for the 2 months already booked. When New Zealand went into lockdown, the Whakatane couple found them a relative's apartment and a car for the month it took to get a flight home.

The cost of renting a comparable commercial motorhome for 2 or 3 months at a time could be substantial. Here, the owners exchanged the use of assets they already possessed, although travel, operating expenses, and insurance still had to be covered. That is the model at its most convincing, and it is also published on RV Worldwide's own site. Even Barbara and Mike's first report carried a warning: insuring their visitors was difficult and expensive, because the New Zealanders didn't hold British driver's licenses and needed their own breakdown cover.

The downside: RV Worldwide functions principally as a matching service. The owners remain responsible for the exchange agreement, insurance arrangements, and practical details; the company suggests that each owner make sure their vehicle is insured while the partner drives it, and it supplies a sample exchange agreement on request. Its relatively modest membership count also means availability may be limited in a particular destination.

2. Swap My Van — The Free-Spirited Alternative

Swap My Van

Free registration and owner contact

An accessible, map-based swapping community for campervan owners who want to explore international possibilities without paying a membership fee.

swapmyvan.com

If RV Worldwide feels like an established travel club, Swap My Van feels more like a gathering of van-life enthusiasts who have collectively realized that the world doesn't need another expensive rental agreement. Its approach is refreshingly uncomplicated. Register your vehicle, upload photographs, describe your availability, and browse other campervans using an interactive map and destination filters. Find somebody interested in an exchange, start a conversation, and work out the arrangements.

The platform advertises free registration and communication, with no membership fee required to contact other owners. This could be particularly appealing to younger campervan owners who have invested in their own builds. Imagine spending 2 years transforming an old Volkswagen Transporter into the perfect weekend machine, then discovering that the little van could effectively become your ticket to driving another owner's camper through Spain.

You haven't sold anything. You haven't rented anything. You've simply found somebody who wants to experience your part of the world as much as you want to experience theirs.

Swap My Van's website features favorable testimonials from users in Seattle, San Francisco, Madrid, and Auckland, describing savings and enjoyable international travel. The site labels them verified reviews, but they are published by the platform itself. I couldn't establish a substantial, independently verified review history for the service, so those experiences should be treated as encouraging rather than definitive evidence of reliability.

The downside: Free matching doesn't necessarily mean a protected exchange. Insurance, damage liability, deposits, and other safeguards need to be independently established between the owners.

3. SwapTheRoad — The Clever One With a Points System

SwapTheRoad

Reciprocal swaps + RoadPoints exchanges

A more flexible approach that lets owners exchange vehicles without necessarily having to trade directly with the same person.

swaptheroad.com

This might be the most interesting system of the 3. The traditional problem with swapping is finding somebody who wants exactly what you have, in the location you live, at the same time you want to visit theirs. You want to drive through Norway. A Norwegian owner wants to visit California. Perfect. Except the Norwegian owner wants to travel in February, you want to travel in August, and neither of you particularly wants to solve the logistical puzzle.

SwapTheRoad tackles this problem with a currency called RoadPoints. Members can still arrange conventional vehicle-for-vehicle exchanges, but they can also make nonreciprocal exchanges. For example, an owner could lend a campervan to another member, earn RoadPoints, and subsequently use those points to borrow a completely different vehicle in another country.

Members receive 2,000 promotional RoadPoints for completing their profile and adding their first vehicle, 600 for the first and 1,400 for the second. Owners set their own point values, with a default of 100 points per day. It's a remarkably clever solution because it reduces the need for 2 people to want precisely the same thing at precisely the same time.

The worked example SwapTheRoad uses on its own site. The default value for any vehicle is 100 RoadPoints a day.

Better still, SwapTheRoad accommodates not only conventional motorhomes but also adventure vehicles, including 4x4s with roof tents and pickups with habitation units. Imagine lending your family campervan to somebody visiting the United States, then using the points you've built up on a compact expedition vehicle for a completely different adventure. The possibilities become considerably more interesting when you're not restricted to exchanging like for like.

SwapTheRoad also advertises optional security-deposit management, a free member certification that checks identity, ownership and insurance, and complementary insurance through RentalCover. These are useful potential safeguards, although none should be mistaken for an automatic guarantee of full coverage.

On its site, testimonials describe successful exchanges, including a roughly 3,000-kilometer (1,860-mile) trip through France, Italy, and Switzerland and a 3-week European trip in May 2024. Again, these are company-published accounts rather than independently authenticated reviews.

The downside: RoadPoints add complexity, and a theoretically attractive point balance is only useful when a suitable vehicle is actually available. Membership formulas and the full cost of any additional protections should be checked before committing.

Part Three: Imoova — The Road Trip That Almost Pays for Itself

Now things get especially interesting. Imagine being told that you could drive a motorhome across the United States for $1 a day. Your immediate reaction would probably be to question the condition of the motorhome, the legitimacy of the offer, and whether the previous owner had disappeared under mysterious circumstances. But this is a genuine logistics model.

Rental companies routinely find themselves with vehicles in the wrong locations. Perhaps a customer collected a motorhome in Los Angeles and returned it to Denver. Perhaps a manufacturer has delivered a fleet of new RVs that must be distributed to rental branches. Or perhaps seasonal travel patterns have left one depot overflowing while another is running short.

Moving those vehicles costs money. Hiring a professional driver costs money. Transporting them on a truck costs money. So why not offer the vehicle to somebody who actually wants to drive it?

Enter Imoova. The company, based in Brisbane, has been relocating vehicles since 2007 and runs a marketplace connecting travelers with more than 200 rental companies that need cars, campervans, and motorhomes moved between locations. The advertised daily rate can be as little as $1, and the marketplace currently covers the United States, Canada, Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and Japan.

Instead of renting a motorhome at the usual commercial rate, you're effectively providing a vehicle-delivery service in exchange for very inexpensive use of the machine. Some deals include fuel allowances, ferry crossings, or other incentives.

The concept is ingenious because everyone potentially wins. The rental company gets its vehicle repositioned. The traveler gets a road trip for a fraction of the usual rental cost. And the vehicle is doing exactly what it was built to do.

The catch: This is a delivery with a vacation attached

The vehicle has to arrive at a specific destination, usually within a fixed period. Sometimes that means several days to cross a significant portion of a country. You may have limited time for detours, and Imoova's listings say the vehicle is allocated at pickup, so the precise model may not be known until you collect it. Imoova itself notes that relocations can be canceled and that ordinary travel expenses remain the driver's responsibility, and walking away can be expensive: one archived Imoova listing I checked carried a $1,500 penalty if the renter failed to complete the relocation on the agreed terms.

This is not necessarily the best way to spend 3 leisurely weeks wandering through the French countryside. But for the right traveler, it is fantastic, and independent accounts suggest that the savings are real.

Katie Genter, writing for The Points Guy, has driven 2 relocation motorhomes at $1 a day, Las Vegas to Denver in 2018 and Los Angeles to Dallas in the summer of 2020 (about $1.30 a day in 2026 money). On the first, the rental company reimbursed her fuel and added a $100 travel allowance (about $135 today). The best of these deals often start at the factory. Apollo, El Monte, and Road Bear release factory relocations every spring, and a brand-new motorhome usually starts its life in northern Indiana, around Elkhart, a few hours from a major airport.

Fuel is the bill that $1 doesn't cover. A big motorhome rarely sees much better than 10 mpg, so a 1,500-mile run at November's national average of $4.17 a gallon comes to about $625 in gasoline unless the listing includes an allowance. In other words, don't confuse inexpensive with unrestricted.

A $1 motorhome that has to cross 1,500 miles in 4 days is a tremendous deal if you enjoy driving. It is considerably less appealing if your definition of a vacation involves sleeping until noon and deciding what to do after lunch.

Share of all reviews by star rating, checked November 3, 2026. Ratings change. Trustpilot notes that Imoova hasn't invited customers to review it recently, so the sample may not be representative. Source: Trustpilot.

Imoova has a meaningful independent review trail, unlike the smaller exchange platforms, and the results are mixed but revealing. One reviewer in October 2026 described an excellent 1-week Vancouver-to-Calgary relocation in a roadsurfer campervan. Others praised the low cost and condition of their vehicles.

On the other hand, complaints include mismatched bookings, disagreements over deposits and insurance, late cancellations, and additional costs for essential items such as bedding and cooking equipment. Some of these problems appear to involve the rental companies fulfilling bookings rather than Imoova alone. That distinction matters, although it is little consolation to a customer standing in a rental depot without the campervan they expected.

The conclusion is not to avoid the concept. It is to remember that the quality of an Imoova experience depends heavily on the actual rental operator providing the vehicle.

Carveyance verdict: The best option here for adventurous travelers who don't already own an RV, and perhaps the most entertaining way to turn an otherwise ordinary cross-country journey into a memorable motoring experience.

Part Four: Shipping Your Own RV — Because Sometimes Only Yours Will Do

Swapping is clever. Relocation deals are fantastic. But there is another type of traveler altogether: the person who spent 5 years building an expedition camper with upgraded suspension, a custom electrical system, enough solar panels to power a small village, and a kitchen organized with the precision of a Swiss watch.

That person is not particularly interested in borrowing somebody else's vehicle. They want their own. And, remarkably, there are companies dedicated to making that possible.

American Lamprecht — International Logistics for Your Home on Wheels

American Lamprecht, based in Baltimore, specializes in international vehicle logistics, including recreational vehicles, motorhomes, and automobiles. The company advertises more than 50 years of RV and automotive shipping experience, to destinations across North America, Asia, Europe, and beyond.

For an American owner considering an extended European tour, a freight forwarder can help coordinate the process of getting a vehicle overseas, including the relevant shipping arrangements and customs requirements. It's not as simple as dropping your campervan at a port and showing up in Paris a week later, but specialist transport companies handle the logistics that would make this endeavor intimidating for most private owners.

SeaBridge — For People Who Think Continents Are Just Very Large Road Trips

SeaBridge is particularly interesting because its business is closely connected to the culture of long-distance motorhome travel. The German company has operated since 1997 and reports having shipped more than 15,000 motorhomes overseas.

SeaBridge advertises roll-on/roll-off shipping, road insurance assistance, and routes serving North America, South America, Europe, Southern Africa, Australia, and New Zealand, with American ports including Los Angeles, Seattle, and Baltimore. It also organizes motorhome tours, in your own vehicle or a rented one, although its tour catalog is published in German.

The appeal is obvious. Imagine owning an expedition-ready Mercedes Sprinter camper in California, shipping it to Europe, and spending several months exploring countries that you previously knew only through photographs. Or taking your own vehicle into Africa and driving through Namibia, where the experience isn't simply about reaching your destination. It's about the vehicle that carries you there.

RoRo shipping involves driving the vehicle onto a specialized vessel, securing it for the voyage, and driving it off at the destination. Container shipping is another possibility for vehicles that fit within the relevant dimensions. But costs are considerably higher than swapping, and international shipping introduces customs, temporary import rules, port fees, marine insurance, potential damage, and the possibility of delays.

There is also an important distinction between a shipping company with extensive logistics experience and a guarantee of a flawless experience. Neither American Lamprecht nor SeaBridge had a sufficiently substantial independent RV-customer review sample in my research to justify ranking their customer satisfaction against the other services.

Carveyance verdict: Shipping makes the most sense when the vehicle itself is central to the adventure, especially for extended or specialized expeditions. For an ordinary 2-week vacation? Renting or swapping is probably the more practical choice.

Part Five: Which Approach Makes the Most Sense?

These companies aren't all direct competitors. They're different solutions to the same problem.

RV WorldwideOwner-to-owner exchanges; $79.90/yearLonger international trips planned well ahead

Platform information checked November 3, 2026. Fees, inventory, routes, and exchange conditions may change.

And this is where it becomes fun. Consider 3 hypothetical trips.

Scenario A: 8 weeks exploring New Zealand

You own a California campervan and find a New Zealand owner interested in an exchange. The obvious choice is RV Worldwide or SwapTheRoad. You arrange a long-duration swap, purchase your flights, and avoid an extended commercial rental bill.

Scenario B: A spontaneous American road trip

You don't own an RV, but you've found an appealing one-way route and have a flexible schedule. Imoova is the obvious contender. You accept the time constraints in exchange for potentially remarkable rental savings.

Scenario C: 4 months exploring Europe in your own camper

You have an extensively customized vehicle and don't want to leave it behind. SeaBridge or American Lamprecht becomes much more attractive. Shipping may be expensive, but over a sufficiently long trip, the economics deserve serious consideration against extended rental costs.

Part Six: How Much Could You Actually Save?

Let's take that first scenario: 8 weeks in New Zealand. The following is an illustrative budget, not a live rental quotation. Suppose a comparable commercial motorhome costs $175 per night for 56 nights.

Assumes a successful swap. Flights, fuel, campground fees, insurance, maintenance, security arrangements, rental taxes and fees are excluded. A swap is not guaranteed, and this is not a verified savings quote.

That's an extraordinary theoretical difference. Of course, a real exchange may involve reciprocal wear and tear on both owners' vehicles, additional insurance, cleaning, mileage allowances, and other considerations. It also requires finding a compatible, trustworthy partner.

But even if the eventual savings were substantially less, the fundamental economics remain compelling. You already own a vehicle that costs money whether you use it or not, and an exchange potentially turns that dormant asset into travel value.

Part Seven: The Important Questions Nobody Should Ignore

All of this sounds almost too good to be true, and some of the details deserve more scrutiny than a cheerful website testimonial. A few things should be settled before anybody hands over a key:

  • Insurance: Does the actual policy expressly cover the other driver, country, usage, and exchange arrangement? A normal personal RV policy may not.
  • Damage and liability: Who pays for accidents, deductibles, mechanical damage, repairs, roadside assistance, and diminished value?
  • Mileage and condition: Establish mileage limits, photographs, mechanical condition, equipment inventory, and rules about repairs before departure.
  • Licensing: Confirm that the visitor's license is valid and suitable for the weight and class of vehicle.
  • Cancellation: Determine what happens when one person changes plans, or a relocation supplier withdraws a vehicle after flights have been purchased.
  • International requirements: For shipping, verify import permissions, customs paperwork, temporary admission limits, registration, local insurance, and return-shipping plans.

The most important distinction is that a matching platform, an insurer, a freight forwarder, and a rental supplier perform very different jobs. A company introducing you to another RV owner does not automatically assume legal or financial responsibility for what happens to the vehicle.

And with relocations, the marketplace listing and the supplier's actual rental agreement should match before making nonrefundable travel commitments. This is one of those cases where the paperwork deserves almost as much attention as the itinerary.

Part Eight: 3 More Companies Worth Knowing

Researching the original 6 led to 3 additional services that deserve attention. All 3 work on the same principle as Imoova, each with its own twist.

Transfercar

Alternative to Imoova

One-way relocations with advertised free rental days and, the company says, no booking fee. Its North American listings have centered on routes between Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Las Vegas, with extra days, where offered, at roughly $70 to $150 a day. It also runs in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and South America, and fuel and other travel costs still apply.

transfercarus.com

roadsurfer

Low-cost one-way promotions

Its roadsurfer Rally program advertises one-way campervan trips from $149 a booking, typically 7 days, with 25% extra miles or 125 miles per rental day, whichever is greater. Every Rally route listed on November 3, 2026, started in Europe. Closer to home, roadsurfer is waiving its one-way fee from Los Angeles to Dallas, Miami, or Las Vegas through December 31, on its Family Finca model only. Not quite the $1 model, but more choice may make the difference between a vacation and a vehicle-delivery marathon.

roadsurfer.com/deals

Movacar

1-euro relocations in Germany

Another company applying the same logistics principle, with one-way rentals from €1 (about $1.12). Its offers are mostly cars and vans on routes inside Germany, usually with 24 hours to reach the destination, and renters must be 21 or older and have held a license valid in Germany for at least a year. Worth checking if a European road trip starts or ends there.

movacar.com

Part Nine: The Bigger Picture — An Entirely Different Way to Own a Vehicle

Perhaps the most fascinating thing about these services isn't the money they can save. It's what they suggest about vehicle ownership itself.

For decades, the recreational-vehicle industry has operated around a fairly straightforward premise: buy a vehicle, take it on vacation, park it at home, and repeat. And in between those vacations? The vehicle sits. Sometimes for weeks. Sometimes for months. In many cases, the vehicle is used for only a fraction of the year.

But an RV exchange changes that equation. A vehicle no longer represents just the geographical limits of where its owner is willing to drive. It represents an opportunity to travel in other people's vehicles around the world. A campervan in California could be worth more to its owner as a gateway to an Australian adventure than as a machine parked on the driveway. That is an extraordinary proposition.

It also has a distinctly automotive appeal. Unlike flying somewhere and staying at a hotel, a campervan offers the freedom to explore the roads between destinations. The little villages. The mountain passes. The neglected coastal highways. The places you stumble upon because you made a wrong turn and decided not to correct it.

You might discover that a compact European camper suits narrow mountain roads better than your oversized American motorhome; RV Worldwide itself warns members that North American vehicles generally run larger than European or Australasian ones. You might find that a rugged Australian 4x4 conversion can reach places your own camper would never survive. Or you might discover that somebody else's carefully maintained, 25-year-old Volkswagen campervan has more charm than a brand-new luxury RV. The machine becomes part of the experience.

And there is another aspect to all this worth appreciating: it rewards people for owning and caring for something. Not for buying something new. Not for constantly upgrading. Not for subscribing to yet another expensive service. But for maintaining a vehicle well enough that somebody else would want to experience it. There is something rather wonderful about that.

Conclusion: The Best Road Trip Might Be Sitting in Somebody Else's Driveway

We tend to think of travel as a question of destinations. Where are we going? What will we see? How much will it cost to get there? But perhaps we've been overlooking something.

The world is already filled with motorhomes, campervans, and adventure vehicles. They're parked in driveways in California, barns in France, garages in New Zealand, and small villages scattered across Europe. Many of their owners dream of visiting exactly the places where somebody else's campervan is sitting idle.

The vehicles already exist. The roads already exist. The desire to travel certainly exists. All that was missing was a practical way of connecting them.

RV Worldwide, Swap My Van, and SwapTheRoad are trying to make that connection possible. Imoova and Transfercar are turning fleet-management headaches into vacation opportunities. And companies like SeaBridge and American Lamprecht are helping particularly determined owners take their own machines across oceans.

None of these systems is perfect. Some require considerable trust and preparation. Others demand flexibility or a willingness to accept logistical uncertainty. But the underlying ideas are undeniably clever.

And in an automotive world increasingly dominated by discussions of horsepower, battery capacity, software, autonomous driving, and resale values, it's refreshing to discover something that celebrates an older, simpler relationship between people and machines. The freedom to go somewhere. Not because you need to. Not because the journey makes financial sense. But because you have a road, a vehicle, and a desire to see what's around the next corner.

Maybe your next great adventure doesn't require purchasing a new motorhome. Maybe it doesn't even require renting one. Maybe all you need is a plane ticket, a little planning, and somebody on the other side of the world who has been dreaming about driving through your part of it. Your driveway might just be the most valuable travel asset you never knew you had.

A note on the reviews

The strongest independent customer-review sample belongs to Imoova, and its 4.0 Trustpilot score hides a meaningful share of unhappy reviewers. RV Worldwide publishes a detailed collection of member accounts, but on its own site. Swap My Van and SwapTheRoad publish appealing testimonials, and I couldn't find comparable independent review volumes for either. The shipping companies' operational experience is easier to document than their customers' satisfaction, which is why the accounts in this piece are not presented as equally verified.
